Methodology · built 2026-11-17

Where these figures come from

Every month, the Department of Energy compiles retail electricity rates for each distribution utility by hand, from rate sheets the utilities post as PDFs, web tables and Facebook posts. This prototype turns that compilation into a dataset a machine can join, check and update. This page explains how it was built, what each figure means, and where it falls short.

Every number on this page is computed from the same build as the explorer, so it stays current when the data is refreshed.

What is counted

141 distribution utilities: 21 private investor-owned utilities and 120 electric cooperatives, exactly the rows in DOE's rate sheet, which DOE links from doe.gov.ph. Utilities DOE does not list (some LGU-run systems and economic-zone distributors) are not here.

106 months, Jan 2018 to Oct 2026, for three customer classes (residential, commercial, industrial) plus each utility's blended generation charge. That is 44,838 rate cells, of which 27,534 hold a number. The sheet also has a column for Nov 2026; it is still empty, so it is left out of every figure.

What a rate means

A rate is DOE's figure for what a customer in that class paid per kilowatt-hour that month, in pesos, as DOE entered it. This prototype never edits DOE's numbers.

DOE does not publish how it derives each figure. For Meralco, the residential figure equals the total bill per kWh at 200 kWh of monthly use, as printed in Meralco's own "Residential Bills at Typical Consumption Levels" table. For utilities that publish unbundled charges (generation, transmission, distribution, taxes, subsidies), the method DOE used to arrive at one number is not stated, so this prototype does not try to rebuild it.

The generation charge is the cost of the electricity itself, passed through from power suppliers. It is part of the retail rate, not added to it.

Missing figures

DOE marks a month it has no figure for as NDA (no data available). 38.6% of rate cells are NDA: residential 28.0%, commercial 41.2%, industrial 46.6%; generation charge 44.9%.

Residential gaps have narrowed but not closed: 51.3% of cells in 2018, 5.2% at the lowest (2023), 11.4% in 2026. Off-grid utilities, which serve islands and remote areas, are missing more often (41.8%) than on-grid ones (25.6%). In Oct 2026, 80.1% of utilities have a residential figure.

An NDA month is never treated as zero. It is left out of medians, drawn as a gap in the chart, and hatched on the map.

From sheet to table

The sheet is formatted for people: title rows, region sub-headers, one column per month, and a SOURCES column of links. A script in six steps turns it into tables:

  1. Fetch. Download the four tabs (residential, commercial, industrial, generation) as CSV, and once more as a workbook to keep the SOURCES hyperlinks, which CSV export drops. Every raw file is kept with its URL in a manifest.
  2. Parse. Find the header row, read every row whose type is PIOU or EC, and turn month columns into rows: one row per utility, month and class. Each cell keeps a note saying whether it held a number, NDA, a blank, or something unreadable.
  3. Check the sheet. The four tabs list the same utilities in the same order; any row where they disagree is logged. Values outside 1–40 PHP/kWh and cells that are not numbers are logged too.
  4. Map coverage to PSGC codes (below).
  5. Check against utilities' own documents (below).
  6. Publish CSV, Parquet, a Frictionless datapackage.json, the JSON API and this site.

The code is Python, run with uv run python -m pipeline. Small tests guard the parsing rules most likely to fail quietly.

One ID per utility

Every utility gets a utility_id made from the name DOE prints: meralco, neeco-ii-area-i, leyeco-1-dorelco. It is issued once and kept: each build reads the published master list first, so if DOE later renames a utility, the ID does not change. A new name gets a new ID, and linking it to an old one (after a merger, say) is a deliberate edit, not a guess.

This is the common ID the Energy challenge asks for. It is meant to sit alongside ERC, NEA and DOE's own codes once those are added, not to replace them.

Where each utility serves

No public, machine-readable franchise list from ERC or NEA could be reached for this prototype. Coverage comes from the "Areas served" column of Wikipedia's List of electric distribution utilities in the Philippines (revision 1374171231, 2026-09-10), which cites DOE's utility profiles and Distribution Development Plans. It is a secondary source, the weakest in the set, and the first thing to replace.

Each listed city or municipality is matched to its 10-digit PSGC code from PSA's 2026 publication (via bendlikeabamboo/barangay v2026.10.12.0). The rules are strict on purpose:

  • Where the source names a province ("Samal, Davao del Norte"), only a town in that province can match.
  • A name that fits several towns matches only if exactly one of them lies in a province, or failing that a region, the same utility already serves.
  • Anything else is left unmatched and listed for a person to resolve. Nothing is inferred from a utility's name or region.

1,648 of 1,664 listed places matched; 16 are in qa/unmatched_areas.csv. 86 carry a qualifier from the source, such as "Some areas only" or "Off-the-grid", which is kept. 137 of 141 utilities have province codes; the other 4 serve only independent cities, which belong to no province and carry their own codes.

Checking DOE against the source

The challenge asks for the monthly count to be made automatic. To show what that looks like, scrapers read five utilities' own rate documents for the last 12 months and compare each figure with the number in DOE's sheet. Every comparison, with the source page shown and the figure highlighted, is on the source checks page.

UtilityWhere the figure comes fromHow it is readResult
Meralco The monthly "Residential Bills at Typical Consumption Levels" PDF, listed on the rates archive, e.g. the Oct 2026 PDF Printed: the PHP/kWh table's 200 kWh row, non-lifeline. Its total is the residential rate; its first column is the generation charge. 22 of 46 match (Jan 2018 to Oct 2026)
CELCOR The same kind of table, from the rate archive. The page is a JavaScript app; its file list comes from a JSON API, found by watching the page's network requests. E.g. the Oct 2026 PDF Computed: the 200 kWh row prints pesos, so the total bill ÷ 200 is the residential rate and the generation charge ÷ 200 is the generation charge. 11 of 22 match (Dec 2025 to Oct 2026)
Tarlac Electric The monthly rate schedule PDF, embedded in a page per month, e.g. the Oct 2026 PDF Printed: the Generation Charge row, residential column. Tarlac publishes unbundled charges, and DOE's residential number can't be rebuilt from them without DOE's method, so only the generation charge is compared. 10 of 10 match (Jan 2026 to Oct 2026)
Angeles Electric The monthly bill insert, an image also posted on Facebook, linked from its billing advisories, e.g. the Oct 2026 image Read from the image (below). It prints the change in the residential rate from last month and its components, so it is checked against the change in DOE's figures. 6 of 8 match (Jul 2026 to Oct 2026)
Clark Electric Rate schedule and generation-cost tables as images on its rates page, e.g. the Sep 2026 image Read from the image. The generation charge is compared directly; the schedule's charges at 200 kWh before tax (the formula) are a floor DOE's all-in rate must clear. 39 of 45 consistent (Jan 2020 to Sep 2026)

DOE prints two decimals, so a gap of up to 0.006 PHP/kWh counts as a match. 88 of 131 figures match; 43 differ. 102 more were already published by the utility while DOE's column was still empty.

Where they differ. 43 comparisons differ: Angeles Electric residential (2), Clark Electric residential (6), CELCOR residential (11), Meralco residential (24). Every generation-charge comparison matches. DOE does not publish how it derives a utility's figures, so each difference is a question to put to DOE, not a finding that either number is wrong.

  • CELCOR, residential rate. For Meralco, the 200 kWh bill reproduces DOE's figure to the centavo from Dec 2025 to Oct 2026, so the same reading was applied to CELCOR. For CELCOR it doesn't: DOE's figure is below the 200 kWh bill in 9 of 11 months (by up to 1.37 PHP/kWh) and above it in 2, and in 11 of the 11 differing months no consumption level in CELCOR's table gives DOE's number either. CELCOR's generation charge matches DOE in 11 of 11 months.
  • Angeles Electric, change in the residential rate. AEC's monthly notice states the change from the previous month, so it is compared with the change in DOE's figures. They agree in 2 of 4 months. In Aug 2026, DOE's figure moves +2.89 PHP/kWh while AEC's notice states -0.0019; AEC's components for that month add up to its stated change, and two of its notices print the same figure. Following AEC's own changes from Jul 2026, when both agree, DOE's AEC figure sits 2.71 to 2.89 PHP/kWh higher through Oct 2026. AEC's generation-charge changes match DOE's in every month checked.
  • Clark Electric, residential rate. CEDC publishes a rate schedule, not a bill, so the formula gives its residential charges at 200 kWh before VAT and local taxes; an all-in rate can't be lower. DOE's figure is lower in 6 of 11 months (by up to 3.77 PHP/kWh). In 8 of those 11 months the reader missed some charges that it found in other months (usually the universal charges), which only lowers the floor there, so any gap in those months is understated. CEDC's generation charge matches DOE in 34 of 34 months, and fills a month DOE marks NDA.
  • Meralco, residential rate, older months. Meralco's archive goes back to 2009, so the check also covered the older months where DOE has no generation charge and does have a residential figure. In all 24 of them (Jan 2018 to Dec 2019), DOE's figure differs from Meralco's 200 kWh bill. In 22 of those it equals another row of Meralco's own table exactly: the 400 kWh bill in 21 months, and other levels in 1. So DOE's figures are copied correctly, but at a different consumption level than it uses today, which a series spanning both periods needs to say.

Each figure keeps its evidence: a copy of the file (with its SHA-256, so a changed file is noticed), the page, the row as extracted, and where the row and the value sit on the page. DOE's side links to the exact cell in DOE's Google Sheet. A reviewer can check any row in two clicks.

Not automated yet: Facebook. DOE's SOURCES column links 78 utilities to a website, 54 to a Facebook page and 9 to nothing; 19 of the websites did not load cleanly when checked, and CELCOR's link loads the site's own "Error 404" page. The Facebook-only utilities are covered below. The link audit is published in full.

Tools considered. reverse-api-engineer records a site's network traffic and writes a client for the API behind it. That is the method used, by hand, to find CELCOR's archive API, and it is the right tool for the next utility sites that are JavaScript apps. agent-reach reaches Facebook only for search and page profiles, through a personal logged-in session copied from the user's browser, and is flagged experimental; it doesn't read a Page's posts or photos, where rates are, and running public infrastructure on a personal session breaks Meta's terms.

How a rate is built

Philippine electricity bills are unbundled: by law (the EPIRA, RA 9136) and ERC's rules on the bill format, each charge is shown on its own line. For a customer who uses Q kWh in a month:

bill(Q) = Q × (sum of per-kWh charges)
        + per-customer charges
        + local franchise tax   (a percentage of the charges above)
        + VAT
        − lifeline / senior discounts   (qualified customers only)

effective rate(Q) = bill(Q) ÷ Q
  • Per-kWh charges: generation, transmission (and ancillary services), system loss, distribution, supply and metering, the lifeline and senior-citizen subsidies, the universal charges (missionary electrification, environmental, NPC stranded debt), FIT-All and GEA-All for renewables, and real property tax.
  • Per-customer charges: fixed pesos per month for supply and metering.
  • VAT: 12% on the distribution-side charges. On generation and transmission it is the VAT the suppliers actually billed, which depends on the month's supplier mix (some renewable supply is zero-rated). It can't be rebuilt from the rate schedule alone; utilities print it on their typical bills.

So there is no single "true rate". Because the per-customer charges are spread over Q, the rate changes with use: fixed charges weigh more on small users, low users may get lifeline discounts, and some charges are tiered (in Meralco's 2018 tables the rate per kWh rises with use). The convention is a typical bill at 200 kWh: Meralco publishes it, and DOE's figures for Meralco from Dec 2025 on are exactly that bill ÷ 200. Earlier, DOE read a different row (below).

Checked against a utility's own documents. CELCOR publishes both a rate schedule and its typical bills each month. For October 2026, its residential schedule × 200 kWh reproduces every non-tax line of its 200 kWh bill to the centavo (generation ₱7.5005 × 200 = ₱1,500.10; distribution ₱1.2081 × 200 = ₱241.62; metering ₱5.00 per customer…), and its franchise tax is exactly 0.825% of those charges (₱17.91). Only VAT (₱242.17) has to come from the bill itself. This is a test in the pipeline (pipeline/billcalc.py).

How this site uses the formula: where a utility publishes a typical-bill table, the effective rate is read from it (bill at 200 kWh ÷ 200). Where it publishes only a schedule, as CEDC does, the formula gives the charges before VAT and local taxes, and DOE's all-in figure has to be at least that.

Reading images, and the Facebook-only utilities

Many utilities publish rates as images: infographics, scanned bill inserts, screenshots of tables, Facebook posts. Writing a parser per layout would break the next time a utility redesigns its notice. Instead, any document goes through the same three steps:

  1. OCR finds every word on the page and where it sits (Apple's Vision framework here; Tesseract on a Linux server).
  2. A vision model reads the document into one fixed schema: for each printed figure, what it measures (generation charge, an all-in rate, a component), for which customer class and month, whether it is a level or a change from last month, its unit and consumption basis, and the number exactly as printed. It is told never to compute.
  3. Deterministic checks decide what is trusted. The printed number must be found in the OCR text, which also gives the box the viewer highlights. Components must add up to the stated total; for AEC's notice, the five component changes sum to the stated change in the residential rate. The same figure in two documents must agree. Levels must be plausible. A document that fails goes to review, not into the data.

When a layout changes, nothing in steps 1–3 changes. The fast text parsers for Meralco, CELCOR and Tarlac fall back to this reader if they stop finding their row. Only discovery, which finds each month's document on a utility's site, is per utility, and it is a few lines each. This run read 111 image documents used in the checks into 5,316 figures; 4,709 of them were confirmed by OCR. Each document is read once, cached by its SHA-256.

Facebook. DOE links 54 utilities to Facebook pages. Logged out, a script gets nothing usable: a page answers HTTP 400, and Facebook's public page widget sends an empty shell that loads posts with JavaScript. Getting past that means scraping with a logged-in or headless browser, which Meta's automated-collection terms forbid without permission. A pipeline running on one person's account would also break unattended. The sanctioned routes, in order of how soon they can work:

  1. Now: a hand-off inbox. DOE staff already open these posts every month to copy the numbers. Instead, they save the post's image into data/inbox/<utility_id>/ with its link, and the reader and checks above take it from there. The manual step shrinks from typing numbers to saving a file, and every figure keeps its evidence.
  2. Utilities connect their own Page. A utility's Page admin can grant a DOE- or NEA-registered app read access to the Page's own posts through Meta's Graph API, a one-time step per utility that NEA can ask of the 120 cooperatives. The app then pulls each month's post and image like any other source.
  3. Meta's research access. Page Public Content Access (Graph API, after app review) or the Meta Content Library (for qualified research and nonprofit institutions) give read access to public Pages without each utility acting.
  4. The lasting fix: file it with DOE. A monthly rate filing, in any format, through a DOE upload form or email. The reader above handles whatever arrives, so utilities don't need new tools, only a place to send what they already post.
Problems found in DOE's sheet

The build found 23 problems in the sheet itself: 15 values outside 1–40 PHP/kWh (negative rates, and one figure in the thousands), 7 rows where the tabs disagree about the same utility's grid, region or name, and 1 cell holding a date where a rate should be.

These values stay in the data exactly as DOE entered them, listed in doe_sheet_issues.csv. They are left out of medians, charts and the map. Where the tabs disagree, the master list follows the residential tab.

Medians and comparisons

The national and regional medians are the middle value across utilities with a figure that month. They are unweighted: a cooperative with 20,000 customers counts the same as Meralco with millions. They describe utilities, not households. A customer-weighted average needs customer counts per utility, which this prototype does not yet have from an official source.

A regional median is shown only when the region has at least three utilities; for fewer it would just repeat them. "Versus national" compares a utility's latest figure with the national median for the same month.

The map

Boundaries are PSA's municipal and city areas for PSGC 3Q 2026, from faeldon/philippines-json-maps v1.1.1 at medium resolution (1% of the source vertices), keyed by 10-digit PSGC code. BetterGov's open-data-visualization ships the same set at low resolution; medium is used here because the map zooms in to street level. 1,642 places are drawn.

The street map underneath is OpenFreeMap (OpenStreetMap data), drawn with MapLibre, which this site serves itself. The tiles are the site's only request to another server: no key, no cookies. A checkbox turns them off.

Each place takes the rate of the utility the coverage source lists for it. 55 places are listed under more than one utility; they show the median of those utilities, and the hover lists each. 1,590 places have a utility; 52 have none listed and are outlined, not coloured. A place served by a utility that covers only part of it is marked in the hover and the place panel.

Colours use five fixed bands, so a colour means the same price in every month. Places whose utility has no figure that month are grey, not coloured as cheap. Clicking a place zooms to it and shows who serves it, the rate, how it compares with the national median, and the last three years.

Power interruptions

How often the power goes out comes from the National Electrification Administration's quarterly Compliance Report on the Performance of ECs, listed on its EC Classifications page. Appendix B of each report gives, per electric cooperative, SAIFI (sustained interruptions per customer), SAIDI (minutes without power per customer), system loss, and NEA's compliant or non-compliant flag for each. The reports are text PDFs, so they are parsed directly; the parser stops on any line it doesn't recognise rather than skip it. 10 reports, Q1 2024 to Q2 2026, give 1,208 rows for 121 cooperatives, each joined to the master list's utility_id. NEA's earlier reports are no longer on its website.

Year to date. The figures rise through each year and start again each first quarter, so they read as year to date, and the Q4 2025 figure is the full year. NEA doesn't say so; the data marks the basis as inferred. NEA's yearly standards are 25 interruptions and 2,700 minutes (45 hours) per customer for on-grid cooperatives, 30 and 3,375 off-grid. In 2025, the median cooperative's customers had 11.9 interruptions and 10.8 hours without power (117 cooperatives with a figure; unweighted, as with the rate medians). The longest: BASELCO (275 hours), CASELCO (157 hours), LASURECO (129 hours).

What NEA doesn't print. 50 rows have no figure because the cooperative sent none; NEA prints a code (dns, nds or nda) and flags it non-compliant, so its compliance counts mix unreliable service with missing reports. The explorer says which. 25 year-to-date figures fall from one quarter to the next within a year, which a running total can't do; for example, SIASELCO's 2024 figure falls from 4,227 minutes in Q2 2024 to 2,838 in Q4 2024. They are published as questions for NEA, and the figures are shown as printed.

Private utilities are regulated by ERC, which collects reliability data from them in its reporting template but doesn't publish it, so they show as "not published", not as having no outages. On the map, a cooperative's figure is its average over its whole area, so every place it serves takes the same colour; it doesn't say which towns lose power most.

What this does not tell you
  • Not your bill. A bill depends on how much you use, lifeline and senior discounts, local taxes and arrears. DOE's figure is one rate per class per month.
  • Not an official DOE product. It is an independent prototype built from DOE's public sheet, for the BetterGov Fellowship 2026.
  • Not a franchise record. Coverage comes from a secondary source and should not settle any boundary question.
  • Not weighted by customers, as above.
  • Not suppliers yet. The challenge's master list also covers generation companies and retail electricity suppliers; this prototype covers distribution utilities only.

The compiled data is published under ODC-BY 1.0 and the code under MIT; source data stays under its publishers' terms. The site loads no third-party fonts, scripts, analytics or trackers; its one outside request is the optional street map's tiles.

Run it yourself

Everything here rebuilds from public sources with one command, uv run python -m pipeline, or from the saved snapshots with --offline. The datapackage describes every published file, its fields and keys. The JSON API is documented in OpenAPI 3.1 on the Data & API page.
